clue.text: Prisoner finally does bird over murder (7)

indicators.note: 'finally' means at the end, so it takes the last letter of 'does'
'over' as in turned over, so the bird is flipped back to front

blocks.note: the flightless bird, which 'over' turns round

annotation.surface: A convict serving out his sentence after a killing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Does bird' is slang for serving time, so the prison picture feels complete; 'murder' is the informal sense of polishing off food or drink, as in 'I could murder a curry'.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: to murder a pie or a pint is to eat or drink it greedily.

clue.text: Visual is current with work coming up (7)

indicators.note: 'coming up' means rising, and in a down entry rising means moving to the top of the word

blocks.note: current = TOPICAL; its OP moves up and out, leaving T…ICAL

annotation.surface: A plain statement that something seen is up to date, with some job arriving.
annotation.walkthrough: TOPICAL already contains the work; 'with work coming up' lifts that OP to the head of the down entry, so no letters are added or lost overall.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe things to do with sight.

clue.text: Perhaps Gala lifting sound after struggle? (9)

indicators.note: 'after' means following, so the sound is placed behind the struggle

blocks.note: a scrum is a scuffling crowd or tussle
a ping is a short ringing sound

annotation.surface: A festive gala, with a hoist or lift and a noise after a scuffle.
annotation.walkthrough: Gala is an apple variety, not a festival, and 'lifting' is the slang for stealing; scrumping is the British word for pinching apples from someone's orchard.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional word: in Britain, stealing apples such as Galas from an orchard is called scrumping.

clue.text: I’m upset with this swimming stroke that went wrong (6)

indicators.note: 'upset' as in knocked over, so in a down entry I'M is turned upside down
things that are swimming drift around, so the letters of THIS drift into a new order

annotation.surface: A swimmer is annoyed that her stroke went wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swimming stroke' reads as one phrase about the pool; split them, and 'stroke' belongs to the definition, a shot in golf or cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition: a mishit is a bad shot with a bat, club or racket.

clue.text: Spooner’s old man wagered unrecoverable liability (3,4)

indicators.note: Rev Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version swaps them here

blocks.note: old man = dad, which takes the B from the next word
wagered = bet, which takes the D from dad; the B of debt is silent

annotation.surface: An old father's bet turns into a debt he cannot pay back.
annotation.walkthrough: Swap the D of DAD with the B of BET and the phrase becomes an accountant's term; the surface of a father's losing bet makes the definition feel earned.
annotation.definitionFit: An accounting term: a liability that will never be repaid is written off as this.

clue.text: Deletion of program on phone, wanting space, ok (8)

indicators.note: 'wanting' in its sense of lacking, so the space is missing from the word

blocks.note: a phone program is an app
an em is a printer's space, removed from REMOVAL

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether it is fine to delete an app because the phone is short of storage.
annotation.walkthrough: The em is a typesetter's unit of space. The definition is the noun sense of ok, as in 'give it the OK'.
annotation.definitionFit: Noun sense: giving a plan the OK means giving it your sanction.

clue.text: Tea for one of Doctor Kildare’s first home visits (5)

indicators.note: 'first' picks out the opening letter of Kildare
a visitor goes inside a home, so the home goes inside DR K

annotation.surface: TV's Dr Kildare making a house call and getting a cuppa.
annotation.walkthrough: Dr Kildare was a TV doctor of the 1960s; 'home visits' feels like one idea, but the home is what does the visiting.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: 'for one' means 'for instance', and tea is one instance.

clue.text: Part of town that’s revolting – King taken by surprise at the outset (7)

indicators.note: something taken by another is held by it, so the king sits inside the surprise
'outset' is the start, so that piece goes first

blocks.note: boo, the cry that startles someone

annotation.surface: A monarch shocked to find a district of town in revolt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' suggests an uprising, but it means disgusting, and the word you say at something disgusting supplies the ending.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition: a borough is an administrative district of a town or city.

clue.text: E.g enthuse defender with say, 4-4-2 (4-9)

blocks.note: a back is a defensive player in football
4-4-2 is a football formation; 'say' flags an example

annotation.surface: A football coach getting a defender excited about playing 4-4-2.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enthuse' looks like an instruction to cheer on the defender, but it is the definition's example: the verb was made by trimming the older noun enthusiasm.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: enthuse is a linguist's textbook case of a word formed backwards from a longer one.

clue.text: Wind in America goes the other way (1-5)

indicators.note: 'in' means inside, so the wind is placed within America

blocks.note: to wind is to turn, as a road winds

annotation.surface: A weather report about American winds changing direction.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wind' reads as moving air, but it is the verb that rhymes with 'find': to twist.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: making a U-turn is reversing direction.

clue.text: A power tool they hope to get in (8)

annotation.surface: Hopefuls queuing to get hold of a power tool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Power tool' looks like one item, a drill perhaps; split it and power is a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic-style description: people who apply for a place or job are hoping to be admitted.

clue.text: Thick walls collapsing here in ancient Rome (3)

indicators.note: a word's walls are its outside letters, and collapsing walls fall away

blocks.note: THICK without its outer letters T and K

annotation.surface: Thick walls falling down in the ruins of ancient Rome.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ancient Rome' signals Latin: the answer is the Latin word, not English.
annotation.definitionFit: A foreign word: the Romans said this for 'here'.

clue.text: Seafood swindle pursued by detective (6)

indicators.note: something pursued has its pursuer behind it, so the detective follows the swindle

annotation.surface: A seafood fraud being chased by a private eye.
annotation.walkthrough: Scampi, breaded langoustine tails, is a British pub-menu staple, which is why it sits so easily next to a swindle.
annotation.definitionFit: A hypernym: scampi is one particular seafood dish.

clue.text: Available after pound fell (5,3)

indicators.note: 'after' means coming later, so available is placed behind pound

blocks.note: to pound is to knock hard
out = available, as a newly released book

annotation.surface: Something became available after sterling dropped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pound fell' reads as a currency slide; pound is really the verb, and fell is the verb meaning to strike down.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: felling a boxer with one punch leaves them flat and unconscious.

clue.text: Quietly ring back to get checked (5)

definitions.note: PLAID is used adjectivally here, as in a plaid shirt.

indicators.note: 'back' as in going backwards, so the ring is read from right to left

blocks.note: to ring someone is to dial them

annotation.surface: Discreetly phoning back to have something checked out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Checked' reads as verified, but it describes a pattern of squares, like tartan cloth.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective sense: a plaid shirt has a tartan pattern of crossing stripes.

clue.text: Record a beat on the radio, calculating power (9)

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so the words go in by their sound

blocks.note: a beat = a rhythm, written by its sound

annotation.surface: Recording a beat broadcast on radio, with a nod to computing power.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Calculating' reads as an adjective about power, but together the two words describe an exponent used in sums.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical description: this is the power to which a base must be raised to give a number, once used for calculating.

clue.text: Disguised gin with tonic swirling round (9)

indicators.note: a swirled drink has its contents stirred about, so the letters are too

annotation.surface: Someone in disguise with a gin and tonic swirling in the glass.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swirling round' reads as one phrase about the glass; round is not part of the indicator but supplies a letter shaped like a ring.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone travelling with their identity hidden is in disguise.

clue.text: One fifth of thirteen going into 26 freely without fractions (8)

indicators.note: read literally, the fifth letter of thirteen
going into something means joining it, so I and T join the other letters
letters used freely are not held to their order

annotation.surface: A maths problem: a fifth of thirteen divided into 26, not allowing fractions.
annotation.walkthrough: The numbers are a maths trap: 'fifth of thirteen' is a letter, and 26 points to the answer at 26 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A mathematical sense: an integral value is a whole number.

clue.text: Produce – and handle – Elton John for instance (5,4)

blocks.note: to stage a show is to produce it
a handle is slang for a name

annotation.surface: Producing and managing Elton John's career.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like managing a star; it is slang for a name.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the singer was born Reginald Dwight and performs under another name.

clue.text: Best team to make cut (7)

annotation.surface: The strongest squad making the cut for a tournament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Make the cut' suggests selection; cut is the butcher's sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A hypernym, with a British butchery term: this is a lean joint of beef from the hindquarter, used for roasting.

clue.text: Threatening look from member of parliament on select committee for starters (5)

indicators.note: starters come first, so take the first letters of select committee
'on' as in next to, so the owl joins SC

blocks.note: a group of owls is a parliament

annotation.surface: An MP glowering at a select committee hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Member of parliament' is not an MP: a parliament is the collective noun for a group of owls.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a dark, angry frown directed at someone.

clue.text: Little fib about husband’s bike stunt (7)

indicators.note: 'about' as in around, so little wraps round the husband

annotation.surface: Someone telling a white lie about their husband's motorbike trick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Little fib' reads as one phrase, but the two words are separate pieces, and 'about' works on little alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition: riding a bike on its back wheel with the front raised.

clue.text: Jaunty part of anorak is hood (6)

indicators.note: 'part of' means a piece of, so the answer is a piece of the words that follow

annotation.surface: A claim that the hood is the stylish part of an anorak.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to describe a coat; the letters run across three words from the end of anorak.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dashing and a little devil-may-care in style.

clue.text: Rival Pope made strange claims about religious books (8)

indicators.note: something made strange is changed from its usual form, so POPE is rearranged
to claim is to take, so the jumbled Pope takes ON inside

annotation.surface: An antipope making odd claims about scripture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Claims about' looks like 'makes claims concerning'; claims actually means takes in, and about is a separate two-letter word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone on the other side of a contest.

clue.text: Different gold-plated article (5)

indicators.note: plating is a coating on the outside, so gold goes round the article

annotation.surface: A distinct item that has been gold-plated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Article' reads as an object; here it is the grammatical article.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: not the same one, but a distinct one.

clue.text: Hulk director’s detailed tip to actor – one with a line? (6)

indicators.note: read as de-tailed: with its tail, the last letter, cut off
a tip is an end, so take the last letter of actor

blocks.note: Ang Lee directed Hulk (2003); ANGLEE loses its tail
the tip of actor is its last letter

annotation.surface: A film director giving an actor a detailed note about a line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' means thorough in the surface but is read as de-tailed. The line is a fishing line, not a script, which the question mark flags.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a fisherman is someone holding a rod and line.

clue.text: When half-cut, draw back tattoo (3)

indicators.note: read literally, half of the word is cut away

blocks.note: draw back = SHRINK; its first half is cut off

annotation.surface: A drunk getting a tattoo, then shrinking away from it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which is why the surface is a boozy tattoo; here it means SHRINK loses its first three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A modern slang verb: tattooists speak of getting inked.

clue.text: Heriot Watt, Edinburgh ultimately struggling until now (8)

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means in the end, so take the last letters of Watt and Edinburgh
something struggling is thrashing about, so the letters are in disorder

blocks.note: last letters of Watt and Edinburgh

annotation.surface: Heriot-Watt, a university in Edinburgh, has had a hard time so far.
annotation.walkthrough: Heriot-Watt is a real Edinburgh university, which makes the names look fixed; 'ultimately' applies to both Watt and Edinburgh.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: up to this point in time.

clue.text: Frosty Spike Milligan scene with actor, Oliver Reed taking only seconds (6)

indicators.note: take only the second letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: Milligan scene with actor, Oliver Reed
blocks.note: mIlligan sCene wIth aCtor oLiver rEed

annotation.surface: A cold comedy sketch with Spike Milligan and Oliver Reed that was over in seconds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frosty Spike' looks like a nickname for Spike Milligan, the comedian; the definition is a spike of ice.

clue.text: Drunkenly mess up one line, using skirts to monkey around (7)

indicators.note: a skirt is an edge, so the skirts of monkey are its outer letters
'around' means surrounding, so MY goes round the rest

blocks.note: the skirts of MONKEY are M and Y
to err is to make a mistake

annotation.walkthrough: Merry is British for tipsy, which is how the adverb fits 'drunkenly'.
annotation.definitionFit: A British sense: merry means pleasantly drunk, so the adverb means tipsily.

clue.text: Maybe Magnum’s close to his nose (7)

indicators.note: a close is an end, so take the end letter of his

annotation.surface: TV detective Magnum's moustache sitting just under his nose.
annotation.walkthrough: Magnum looks like the TV private eye; it is a Magnum revolver.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, using slang: a Magnum revolver is a gun.
